newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-ICA sees factory building boom.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ICA sees factory building boom.

text.p: Amid widespread malaise in Mexico's infrastructure construction sector, leading building firm Empresas ICA has switched its focus to building industrial plants and sees a rosy year ahead in 1997.

In a recent interview with Reuters, Sergio Montano, ICA's executive vice president of finance and administration, said industrial construction now accounts for 40 percent share of the firm's revenues in the first nine months of the year, from 25.6 percent in the previous period.

Faced with what it expects to be a drought of large-scale infrastructure projects in Mexico in 1997, as the country struggles out of economic crisis, ICA has turned its eyes abroad, to projects like the Bakun dam in Malaysia and road building in Panama and Venezuela. It expects these to provide some $660 million to ICA revenues in the next five years or so, Montano said.

"The objective of ICA up to the year 2000 is for a third of its revenues to come from national construction, a third from international construction and a third from infrastructure operation and other business," he said.

In the third category is ICA's bid, with Union Pacific Corp, for Mexico's Northeast railroad operating concession. The winners of the privatization bid were due to be announced late Thursday afternoon.
If ICA's bid wins, its first payment for 40 percent of the cost would come partly via a loan from the financial company Inbursa, Montano said.
The rest would come from its own coffers and loan offers from some 10 other banks, he added.
He said currently the firm is comfortable with its huge cash position of 1.96 billion pesos, $200 of which are held in dollars.

As for financing, he said most of the company's road building projects abroad would be funded on a "project-risk" basis, in which loans are issued and repaid subject to the success of the contract (was contact).He said these loans would not appear on its balance sheet.

In Latin America, he said ICA could handle any contract alone. But in mega-projects outside of the continent, he said it would continue to have a minority stake as it does in the Malaysian Bakun venture.
Infrastructure projects, meanwhile, have shrunk to 28 percent from 38 percent for the comparable periods.

"Next year...we don't see heavy infrastructure projects that are likely to give us an important increase in heavy construction sales," he said. On the other hand, "industrial construction is very good, it has been what has kept up the healthy sales volume and we think we can maintain that."

In 1996, the firm estimates total sales volume of some 7.5 billion pesos, up around 30 percent in nominal terms from 1995. Its backlog, or work in progress, is expected to be around 6.3 billion pesos, equivalent to about 10 months work.
In 1997, ICA calculates that its revenues could rise between 10 and 15 percent in real terms.

In Mexico, ICA has formed alliances with General Electric Co and Site Energy to bid for a power plant project, Merida III. It is also in talks with local rival Bufete for a joint bid to expand the oil refinery Cadereyta, near the northern city of Monterrey.
On the industrial construction front, it has linked up with Fluor Daniel, an alliance that Montano said was aimed at chipping away at Bufete's lead in that area.

Meanwhile, private contracts have overtaken public sector ones as the main source of ICA's revenues -- a turn of events that ICA, which has built an average of one dam a year in its 49 years of existence, does not expect to continue.
"It is not going to be big (private) capital that (contracts me) to build a hydroelectric plant. In Mexico, my number one client is the government," Montano said.
